implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one long-lived hub object owns a registry keyed by event type (class, name, topic), publishers hand their event to the hub, and the hub fans the event out to the subscribers registered for that key (and, if the design generalises, also to the coarser parent keys). Subscribers receive an unsubscribe handle when they register, and the hub owns the threading, filtering and error-isolation policy. Keep the payload immutable, dispatch over a snapshot of the registry so handlers may subscribe or unsubscribe during dispatch, and decide the reference policy (weak vs strong) explicitly. The hub must be the only place that knows the wiring; the moment publishers start calling subscribers directly the pattern has been abandoned. For high-fan-out systems, add a subscriber supervisor that can disable dispatch during write operations to prevent event storms.
code_sketch:
hub.subscribe(event_type, handler) -> token
token.unsubscribe()

hub.publish(event):                    # event carries its type and payload
    for handler in snapshot(registry[event.type]):
        try: handler(event)            # isolated: one failure must not stop the fan-out
        except Exception as e: hub.on_handler_error(e, handler, event)

# Event storm prevention:
hub.disable_dispatch()                # suppress publish() during a batch write
try:
    save_operation()
    hub.flush_pending()                # dispatch suppressed events after commit
finally:
    hub.enable_dispatch()
pitfalls: Publishing from inside a handler without a defined re-entrancy rule turns the hub into a cascade engine.
A registry that is not snapshotted (or a lock held during dispatch) makes subscribe/unsubscribe inside a handler a crash or a deadlock.
Strong references to subscribers that never unsubscribe keep whole object graphs alive - the leak the hub is supposed to prevent.
Synchronous fan-out on a UI thread couples the publisher to every handler's latency; use async/background dispatch for I/O-bound handlers.
No subscriber-supervisor guard: a save-triggered handler that publishes creates an unbounded cascade when the same hub dispatches the re-published event back to the original handler (event storm).
Anonymous lambdas as handlers cannot be unsubscribed unless the original token is retained, silently accumulating stale entries.

Wrong move: relying on reflection-based subscriber registration and never wiring the dead-event channel -> a renamed event type posts into silence with no compile error (Guava EventBus routes by parameter type at runtime) -> instead log or alarm on dead/unrouted events and prefer typed, compile-checked event contracts.

Wrong move: one process-wide bus for all cross-component traffic (the Vue 2 'new Vue()' global bus) -> event-name collisions and invisible data flow make the app unmaintainable, which is why Vue 3 removed the instance emitter API -> instead scope one small bus per feature (e.g. a mitt instance) or use provide/inject or a store for shared state.

Wrong move: choosing an in-process hub for flows that need replay, backpressure or delivery across processes -> the hub copies every event synchronously and loses everything on restart -> instead pick reactive streams (RxJava, Project Reactor, Kotlin Flow) or a messaging channel, as Guava's own wiki now recommends for new EventBus-style designs.
